notes.b: The Consumer Rights Act 2022 sets out statutory rights and remedies for consumers who buy goods, services or digital content from traders.
points: A trader is a person who supplies goods, services or digital content in the course of business.
A consumer is an individual acting for purposes that are not part of their business.
Statutory rights apply automatically to every contract between a trader and a consumer, whether or not the trader mentions them.
A trader cannot remove statutory rights through terms and conditions or notices; a 'no refunds' sign does not override the Act.
Digital content, such as downloaded software, music or films, is covered by the same standards of quality, fitness and description as goods.

notes.b: Goods must meet four standards at the time they are supplied.
points: Satisfactory quality: goods should be durable, safe, free from minor defects, and have an acceptable appearance and finish.
Fit for purpose: goods must be fit for the purposes for which goods of that type are normally used, and for any particular purpose made known to the trader.
As described: goods must match any description given by the trader, the label or the advertisement.
Correspond to sample or model: goods must match a sample or model shown to the consumer before purchase.
A fault that is present when the goods are supplied is the trader's responsibility, even if it appears only later.

notes.b: Services are measured against the standard of a competent provider.
points: Reasonable care and skill: a service must be performed with the care and skill a competent provider would show.
Materials: any materials used in a service must be of satisfactory quality and fit for their purpose.
Time: a service must be performed within a reasonable time where no time was agreed.
Price: where no price was agreed, the consumer pays a reasonable price for the service.

notes.h: Remedies under the Consumer Rights Act 2022
notes.b: Remedies for goods and services that do not meet their statutory standard are applied in a set order.
points: First remedy for goods: repair or replacement at the trader's cost, within a reasonable time and without significant inconvenience to the consumer.
Second remedy for goods: a price reduction or a refund, where repair or replacement is not possible, is not carried out within a reasonable time, or causes significant inconvenience.
Short-term right to reject: faulty goods can be rejected within 30 days of supply and the consumer receives a full refund.
Services that are not performed to the required standard can be re-performed or result in a price reduction.

notes.b: Sale goods have the same statutory rights as other goods, with one exception based on what the consumer was told before buying.
points: Goods bought in a sale are covered by the same statutory rights as goods bought at full price.
Exception: a fault that the trader pointed out before the sale is not covered by the statutory rights for that fault.
A consumer who was not told of a fault before purchase keeps the full statutory remedies for it.

notes.h: Consumer Protection Act 2007: unfair commercial practices
notes.b: The Act prohibits commercial practices that are unfair to consumers, including advertising and selling practices.
points: Misleading actions: giving false or deceptive information about a product, its price, its origin or the trader's identity.
Misleading omissions: leaving out material information that a consumer needs in order to make a decision.
Aggressive practices: harassment, coercion, undue influence or pressure that limits the consumer's freedom to choose.
Prohibited practices: a list of practices banned outright, such as falsely claiming that a product has an approval it does not have.
The Act is enforced by the Competition and Consumer Protection Commission, which can investigate and prosecute offences.

notes.h: Consumer Protection Act 2007: misleading price claims
notes.b: Price claims must be accurate, including claims about reductions and comparisons.
points: False or misleading information about the price of goods or services is prohibited.
A claimed previous price or a claimed reduction must be accurate; a false or misleading reduction is an unfair practice.
A recommended retail price must not be used misleadingly to suggest a saving the consumer would not in fact make.

keyTerms.definition: A person who supplies goods, services or digital content in the course of business.
A right given by law that applies automatically to a contract and cannot be removed by the trader's terms.
The standard that goods should be durable, safe, free from minor defects and acceptable in appearance and finish.
The standard that goods must be suitable for their usual use, or for a particular purpose made known to the trader.
Data produced and supplied in digital form, such as downloaded software, music or films.
A commercial practice in which material information that a consumer needs is left out, so that the consumer decides wrongly.
A commercial practice that uses harassment, coercion, undue influence or pressure to limit a consumer's freedom to choose.
A remedy in which the consumer pays less for goods or services that do not meet the statutory standard.

factCards.term: Order of remedies for faulty goods
factCards.definition: Repair or replacement first; a price reduction or refund if these are not possible or fail.

factCards.term: Four standards that goods must meet
factCards.definition: Satisfactory quality, fitness for purpose, matching the description, and matching any sample or model.

factCards.term: Time limit for rejecting faulty goods outright
factCards.definition: Within 30 days of supply, faulty goods can be rejected and the consumer receives a full refund.

factCards.term: Two types of misleading price information forbidden by the Consumer Protection Act 2007
factCards.definition: False or misleading information about the price itself, and false or misleading information about previous prices or recommended retail prices.

factCards.term: Categories of practice the Consumer Protection Act 2007 treats as unfair
factCards.definition: Misleading actions, misleading omissions, aggressive practices, and practices prohibited outright.

questions.prompt: Explain how the Consumer Rights Act 2022 protects a consumer who buys an appliance that develops a fault shortly after purchase.
questions.model: Goods must be of satisfactory quality and fit for purpose when supplied, and a fault present at supply is the trader's responsibility even if it appears later. The consumer can require repair or replacement at the trader's cost, within a reasonable time and without significant inconvenience. If repair or replacement is not possible or is not carried out, the consumer can take a price reduction or refund. Within 30 days of supply the consumer can reject the faulty appliance and receive a full refund. Statutory rights cannot be removed by a sign or the terms of sale.

questions.prompt: Discuss the statutory rights a consumer has when buying services under the Consumer Rights Act 2022, and explain how the Consumer Protection Act 2007 protects consumers against misleading price claims.
questions.model: Services: the consumer is entitled to a service performed with reasonable care and skill, using materials of satisfactory quality and fit for purpose, within a reasonable time where none was agreed, and at a reasonable price where none was agreed. If the service is not performed to standard, the consumer can require it to be performed again, or obtain a price reduction. These rights apply automatically and cannot be excluded by the trader's terms. Consumer Protection Act 2007: the Act forbids false or misleading information about goods, services and prices. A trader may not claim a previous price or a reduction that is untrue, and may not use a recommended retail price misleadingly to suggest a saving. The Competition and Consumer Protection Commission enforces the Act and can investigate and prosecute offences. A complete answer distinguishes the contract rights given to the consumer from the advertising and pricing controls that protect consumers before purchase.
